The excerpt discusses the technical necessity of specifying a prior for the parameters when using the Bayesian bootstrap, noting that standard bootstrap procedures assume independent and identically distributed data. Because the covariate data comes from a complex survey design, the authors must employ a modified or "scaled" Bayesian bootstrap to correctly account for this non-i.i.d. sampling structure.\n\nTo obtain the posterior distribution of the 𝜑′𝑠, and thus of 𝑃#|%&'(𝑥), we need to specify a prior

for the 𝜑′𝑠. The Bayesian bootstrap is obtained by posing an improper Dirichlet proportional to

∏]8&' 𝜑8L' (sometimes termed Haldane prior). This approach was termed Bayesian Bootstrap by

Rubin (1981) who also describes a straightforward algorithm to sample from the 𝜑′𝑠 posterior.

While postulating a finite support for X is not particularly restrictive, the prior does restrict

analysis to the observed support, in the same way as the frequentist bootstrap.

Due to the complex sampling design, the observations from DHS cannot be considered an iid

sample from X. We consider a BB implementation to account for the complex DHS sampling

design, as detail in the body of the article. While similar BB procedures have been proposed

(Makela et al., 2018; Rao & Wu, 2010; Zangeneh & Little, 2015) we are unaware of a customary

name for the procedure. We termed it the "scaled" or modified BB.

This document details a novel two-step approach combining principal stratification with Bayesian Additive Regression Trees to estimate causal effects in selective samples and generalize those findings to broader populations. The excerpt describes a simulation study designed to test the performance of the proposed scaled Bayesian bootstrap method specifically within the complex sampling design of the Demographic and Health Surveys. This simulation directly supports the methodology section by validating the specialized bootstrap technique required for external validity.\n\nAppendix VII: Simulations and comparisons for the scaled Bayesian bootstrap

We implement a simulation and comparisons to check the performance of the scaled Bayesian

bootstrap in the context of the DHS complex sampling design. Specifically, we compare the

performance of the proposed scaled BB approach with a conventional design-based approach,

which is the standard to conduct inference accounting for DHS complex sampling (Little, 2014).

The covariate age is used as a hypothetical outcome of interest.

_Simulation: DHS sample as a population_

For this simulation, we take the empirical distribution of X in the DHS Nigeria 2018 sample, say

𝐹 [∗] (𝑥), as if it were the distribution in the population exactly. We take repeated samples from this

population using a stratified two-stage cluster procedure as the one used to obtain the DHS

sample, albeit with replacement.

Specifically, for each of the 72 strata, we take a sample of PSUs (the same size as in the DHS)

with probability proportional to size (PPS), using the inverse of the average DHS sampling

weight as a measure of size. For each selected PSU, a sample of respondents is selected by

simple random samplings (SRS), again with the size corresponding to DHS sample (ranging

from 26 to 40, with a median of 28). In both stages, sampling is done with replacement assuming

a small sample fraction (1%). [11]

11 The DHS second stage can involve a larger sample fraction. This information, however, is not publicly released and

cannot be exploited in estimation.

This document details a novel two-step approach combining principal stratification with Bayesian Additive Regression Trees to estimate causal effects in selective samples and generalize those findings to broader populations. The excerpt discusses the imputation of covariates that are only measured in the initial, or "source," sample. It explains that to select conservative imputation values for these missing covariates, the authors calculate a "partial effect" by comparing potential Mean Average Treatment Effects based on varying the imputed covariate's value.\n\nAppendix X: Covariates measured on the source sample only

In this appendix we discuss the selection of the value for imputation of the covariates only

observed in the source sample, i.e., 𝑋! ∖𝑋!. In our application, these covariates are four binary

variables assessing attitudes towards FP. Our goal is to select “conservative” values for

imputation, in the sense that they would result in smaller absolute PATE estimates.

_Partial “effects” of the covariates_

To select a value of a missing covariate for imputation, we calculate a so-called “partial effect”

of the covariate on the MATE (Friedman (2001)), or the “average predictive difference” in terms

of Gelman & Pardoe (2007). This effect or difference is obtained by comparing MATEs based on

varying the imputed value of the missing covariate. While the MATE is a causal quantity (the

causal effect of adopting modern contraceptives on employment), the “partial effect” or “average

predictive difference” of the covariate on the MATE, does not need to be.

Specifically, recall that

This section complements the main text by offering a specific, mathematically defined way to test the robustness of the estimated population average treatment effect when unobserved confounders are present.\n\nAppendix XI: Sensitivity to violation of conditional transportability (assumption 5) –

a parametric approach

The sensitivity analysis in the body of the text avoids parametric assumption about the

unobserved effect modifier. Because the additional flexibility, point identification is lost, and the

interpretation is less straightforward. Here we present an alternative sensitivity analysis in which

we pose a relatively simple parametric model for the unobserved effect modifier. We assume that

Uh is a binary predictor, unrelated with Xh, that affects the CATE’s additively (except near

boundaries, to ensure that CATEs are kept within their range). The model set up can be

summarize as follows,
